html:
The ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid kings, built on a great stone terrace in Fars, the Persian homeland in southwestern Iran. Darius the Great began it around 518 BCE, and his son Xerxes I and grandson Artaxerxes I added to it.

Its halls stood on forests of tall stone columns. The Apadana, the great audience hall, had stairways carved with reliefs of delegations from across the empire, Medes, Lydians, Indians, Ethiopians and others, bringing gifts to the king. Thousands of clay tablets found on site record rations and wages paid to the workers who built it, many from distant lands. It may have hosted the new year festival of Nowruz, though this is debated.

In 330 BCE Alexander the Great took the city and burned the palaces, perhaps in revenge for the Persian burning of Athens. The ruins were never rebuilt. About 90 kilometres away lies Pasargadae, the older capital and tomb of Cyrus the Great. Both are now World Heritage Sites.
